column2: But in the forecourt godly Odysseus lay down to sleep;
beneath he spread an untanned oxhide, and above
many fleeces of sheep, which the Achaeans sacrificed;
and Eurynome threw a cloak over him as he lay.
There Odysseus, with evil thoughts for the suitors in his heart,
lay awake; and from the hall the women
went out, who used to consort with the suitors before,
giving one another laughter and merriment.
His spirit was stirred in his dear breast;
and much he pondered in mind and spirit,
whether to leap after them and bring death to each,
or let them mix once more with the overweening suitors
for the last and latest time; and his heart barked within him.
And as a bitch, standing over her tender whelps,
not knowing the man, barks and is ready to fight,
so his heart barked within him, vexed at the evil deeds;
and striking his chest he rebuked his heart with a word:

Endure, heart; you have endured something even more dog-like before,
19	on that day when the Cyclops of unrestrained might ate
20	my strong comrades; but you endured, until your cunning
21	led you out of the cave, though you thought to die.
So he spoke, chiding the dear heart in his breast;
and his heart held steady in obedience, enduring
unflinchingly; but he himself tossed this way and that.
As when a man turns a paunch over a great blazing fire,
full of fat and blood, this way and that,
and very quickly longs for it to be roasted,
so he tossed this way and that, pondering
how he would lay hands on the shameless suitors,
one man against many. And close to him came Athena,
descending from heaven; and in form she was like a woman;
she stood above his head and spoke a word to him:

Why are you awake again, most ill-fated of all men?
34	This is your house, and this your wife in the house,
35	and your son, such as anyone might wish a son to be.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Yes indeed, goddess, all this you have said in due measure;
38	but this is what my spirit ponders in my mind,
39	how I shall lay hands on the shameless suitors,
40	being alone; and they are always together inside.
41	And besides this, a greater thing I ponder in my mind:
42	for if I kill them, by the will of Zeus and yours,
43	where could I escape? This I bid you consider.
Then the goddess grey-eyed Athena spoke to him in turn:

Hard man, even someone trusts a worse comrade,
46	who is mortal and does not know so many devices;
47	but I am a goddess, who guard you continually
48	in all your labours. And I shall tell you plainly:
49	if fifty companies of speech-endowed men
50	were to stand around us, eager to kill us in war,
51	even of these you could drive off the cattle and fat sheep.
52	But let sleep take you; it is also a vexation to keep watch
53	all night awake, and you will soon come out from your evils.
So she spoke, and poured sleep on his eyelids,
and herself went back to Olympus, the divine one among goddesses.
When sleep seized him, loosing the cares of his heart,
limb-loosening, his wife awoke, knowing kindly things;
and she wept, sitting on her soft bed.
But when she had her fill of weeping in her heart,
to Artemis first the divine one among women prayed:

Artemis, lady goddess, daughter of Zeus, would that now
62	casting an arrow in my breast you would take my life
63	right now, or that a storm wind, snatching me up,
64	would carry me off along the misty paths,
65	and cast me into the mouths of backward-flowing Oceanus.
66	As when the storm winds took away the daughters of Pandareus;
67	their parents the gods destroyed, and they were left
68	orphans in the halls, and divine Aphrodite tended them
69	with cheese and sweet honey and pleasant wine;
70	and Hera gave them beyond all women
71	beauty and wisdom, and pure Artemis gave height,
72	and Athena taught them to do famous works.
73	While divine Aphrodite went to tall Olympus,
74	to ask for the maidens the fulfilment of blooming marriage—
75	to Zeus delighting in thunder, for he knows all things well,
76	both the fortune and misfortune of mortal men—
77	meanwhile the Harpies snatched away the maidens
78	and gave them to the hateful Erinyes to serve.
79	So may they make me vanish, those who hold the Olympian houses,
80	or fair-tressed Artemis strike me, that I may reach
81	beneath the hateful earth with Odysseus before my eyes,
82	and not gladden the mind of a worse man.
83	But this evil has something bearable, when one
84	weeps by day, grieved thickly at heart,
85	and sleep holds him by night—for it makes one forget everything,
86	good and bad, once it has covered the eyelids—
87	but to me a god has sent even evil dreams.
88	For this very night again there slept beside me one like him,
89	such as he was when he went with the army; and my heart
90	rejoiced, for I thought it no dream, but already reality.
So she spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
And as she wept godly Odysseus heard her voice;
and then he pondered, and it seemed to him in his heart
that she, already recognising him, stood at his head.
Gathering the cloak and the fleeces on which he slept,
he put them in the hall on a chair, and the oxhide
he carried outside and put down, and prayed to Zeus, raising his hands:

Father Zeus, if you willingly over land and sea
99	brought me to my own country, after you had afflicted me greatly,
100	let someone of the people waking say a sign for me
101	from within, and outside let another portent of Zeus appear.
So he spoke in prayer; and Zeus the counsellor heard him,
and at once thundered from bright Olympus,
from on high out of the clouds; and godly Odysseus rejoiced.
And a sign from the house a woman grinder sent forth
near by, where the mills of the shepherd of the people were set;
at them twelve women in all were working
making barley-meal and wheat-meal, the marrow of men.
The others were asleep, for they had ground their wheat,
but one was not yet finished, being the weakest;
she, stopping the mill, spoke a word, a sign for her lord:

Father Zeus, who rule over gods and men,
113	surely you thundered loudly from the starry heaven,
114	and nowhere is there a cloud; you show this portent to someone.
115	Fulfil now for me too, wretched, the word that I say:
116	may the suitors on this day, for the last and latest time,
117	take their lovely feast in the halls of Odysseus,
118	they who with heart-grieving toil have loosened my knees
119	making barley-meal; now may they dine for the last time.
So she spoke, and godly Odysseus rejoiced at the omen
and at the thunder of Zeus; for he said he would punish the guilty.
And the other maidservants in the fair house of Odysseus
gathered and kindled on the hearth the unwearied fire.
And Telemachus rose from his bed, a godlike man,
putting on his clothes; and round his shoulder he slung the sharp sword;
and under his shining feet he bound fair sandals,
and took his stout spear, tipped with sharp bronze,
and went and stood on the threshold, and said to Eurycleia:

Dear nurse, did you honour the stranger in the house
130	with bed and food, or does he lie so uncared for?
for such is my mother, wise though she is;
heedlessly she honours one of speech-endowed men
who is worse, and dishonours a better one and sends him away."
Then wise Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:

You should not now, child, blame him who is blameless.
136	For he sat and drank wine, as long as he himself wished,
137	and said he was no longer hungry for food; for she asked him.
138	But when he thought of bed and sleep,
139	she bade the maidservants spread bedding,
140	but he, like one quite wretched and ill-fated,
141	would not sleep on a bed and in rugs,
142	but on an untanned oxhide and fleeces of sheep
143	he slept in the forecourt; and we threw a cloak over him.
So she spoke, and Telemachus went through the hall
holding his spear; and with him two swift dogs followed.
He went off to the assembly among the well-greaved Achaeans.
And she in turn, the divine one among women, called to the maidservants,
Eurycleia, daughter of Ops, son of Peisenor:

Come, some of you sweep the house busily,
150	and sprinkle it, and on the well-made chairs
151	throw purple covers; and others with sponges wipe
152	all the tables, and clean the mixing-bowls
153	and the finely made two-handled cups; and others go
154	to the spring for water, and bring it quickly, going.
155	For the suitors will not be long away from the hall,
156	but will come very early, since it is a festival for all.
So she spoke, and they listened to her well and obeyed.
Twenty of them went to the spring of dark water,
and the others there in the house worked skilfully.
And the attendants of the Achaeans came in. They then
split the wood well and skilfully, and the women
came from the spring; and after them came the swineherd
driving three fatted pigs, which were the best among all.
And these he let feed in the fair enclosures,
and himself spoke to Odysseus with gentle words:

Stranger, do the Achaeans look upon you with more regard at all,
167	or do they dishonour you in the halls, as before?
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Would that, Eumaeus, the gods might repay the insult
170	which these men in their insolence contrive wantonly
171	in another's house, and have no share of shame.
So they spoke such things to one another,
and close to them came Melanthius, the goatherd of goats,
bringing goats which excelled among all the herds,
a dinner for the suitors; and two herdsmen followed with him.
And he tied them up under the echoing portico,
and himself spoke to Odysseus with taunting words:

Stranger, will you still here too be a nuisance in the house,
179	begging from the men, and will you not go out of doors?
180	Altogether I think we two will not be parted
181	before we taste each other's hands, since you do not beg
182	in due order; there are other feasts of the Achaeans too.
So he spoke, and Odysseus of many wiles said nothing to him,
but silently shook his head, brooding evil in the depths of his heart.
And third among them came Philoetius, leader of men,
bringing a barren heifer for the suitors and fat goats.
Ferrymen had brought them across, who also carry
other men, whoever comes to them.
And these he tied up well under the echoing portico,
and himself questioned the swineherd, standing near:

Who is this stranger, swineherd, who has newly come
192	to our house? From what men does he claim to be?
193	Where is his family and his native land?
194	Ill-fated, but in figure he is like a king, a lord;
195	but the gods bring down much-wandering men,
196	when they spin misery even for kings.
He spoke, and standing by he greeted him with his right hand,
and speaking to him addressed him with winged words:

Hail, father stranger; may prosperity be yours hereafter;
200	but now at least you are held in many evils.
201	Father Zeus, no other god is more destructive than you;
202	you do not pity men, when you yourself beget them,
203	to mix them with misery and woeful pains.
204	I broke into sweat when I noticed, and my eyes are filled with tears
205	as I remember Odysseus, since he too, I think,
206	wearing such rags, wanders among men,
207	if he still lives and sees the light of the sun.
208	But if he is already dead and in the house of Hades,
209	ah me then for blameless Odysseus, who set me over the cattle
210	when I was still small in the land of the Cephallenians.
211	And now they have become countless, nor could the breed
212	of broad-browed cattle grow better for any man;
213	but strangers bid me drive them for themselves
214	to eat; and they care nothing for the child in the halls,
215	nor tremble at the gods' vengeance; for they are already eager
216	to divide the possessions of the lord long gone.
217	But this in my dear breast my spirit
218	turns over many times: it would be very bad, while a son is there,
219	to go to the land of others, going with the cattle themselves,
220	to foreign men; but this is more chilling, to stay here
221	sitting with another's cattle and suffer pains.
222	And long ago I would have gone to another of the mighty kings,
223	fleeing, since things are no longer bearable;
224	but still I think of that ill-fated man, if coming from somewhere
225	he might scatter the suitors through the house.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Cowherd, since you seem neither a bad man nor a foolish one,
228	and I myself know that wise understanding has come to you,
229	therefore I will tell you and swear a great oath on it:
230	let Zeus now know first of the gods, and the hospitable table
231	and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come,
232	that while you are here Odysseus will come home;
233	and with your own eyes you will see, if you wish,
234	the suitors killed, who lord it here.
Then the cowherd spoke to him in turn:

Would that, stranger, the son of Kronos might fulfil this word;
237	you would know what my strength is and how my hands follow.
And in the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods
that wise Odysseus might return to his own house.
So they spoke such things to one another,
and the suitors were preparing death and doom
for Telemachus; but a bird came to them on the left,
a high-flying eagle, holding a timid dove.
And Amphinomus made a speech among them and said:

Friends, this plan will not go well for us,
246	the killing of Telemachus; but let us think of the feast.
So spoke Amphinomus, and the speech pleased them.
And going into the house of godly Odysseus
they laid their cloaks on the stools and chairs,
and they sacrificed great sheep and fat goats,
and they sacrificed fatted pigs and a heifer from the herd.
They roasted the innards and distributed them, and mixed wine
in the bowls; and the swineherd handed out the cups.
And Philoetius, leader of men, distributed the bread
in fair baskets, and Melantheus poured the wine.
And they put forth their hands to the ready food set before them.
And Telemachus seated Odysseus, planning shrewdly,
inside the well-built hall, by the stone threshold,
setting a mean seat and a small table;
beside him he put portions of the innards, and poured wine
into a golden cup, and spoke a word to him:

Sit here now among the men, drinking wine;
263	and the taunts and hands of all the suitors
264	I myself will keep off you, since this house is not
265	public, but Odysseus', and he won it for me.
266	But you, suitors, restrain your spirit from rebuke
267	and from hands, that no strife and quarrel arise.
So he spoke, and they all, biting their lips with their teeth,
marvelled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
And among them spoke Antinous, son of Eupeithes:

Let us accept even a harsh word, Achaeans,
272	of Telemachus; he speaks very threateningly to us.
273	For Zeus the son of Kronos did not allow it; otherwise we would already
274	have stopped him in the halls, clear speaker though he is.
So spoke Antinous; but he paid no heed to the words.
And heralds through the town were leading the sacred hecatomb
of the gods; and the long-haired Achaeans gathered
under the shady grove of far-shooting Apollo.
And they, when they had roasted the outer flesh and drawn it off,
dividing the portions, feasted a glorious feast;
and beside Odysseus those who laboured set a portion
equal, as they themselves received; for so bade
Telemachus, dear son of godly Odysseus.
But Athena did not let the proud suitors at all
refrain from heart-grieving insult, so that still more
pain might sink into the heart of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
And there was among the suitors a man who knew lawless things,
Ctesippus was his name, and in Same he had his home;
who, trusting in his marvellous possessions,
wooed the wife of Odysseus, long gone.
He then spoke among the overweening suitors:

Hear me, proud suitors, that I may say something:
293	the stranger has long had his portion, as is fitting,
294	equal; for it is not good nor just to slight
295	the guests of Telemachus, whoever comes to this house.
296	But come, I too will give him a guest-gift, that he himself
297	may give a present to the bath-attendant or to some other
298	of the servants who are in the house of godly Odysseus.
So saying he threw an ox's foot with his stout hand,
taking it from the basket where it lay; but Odysseus avoided it
lightly bending his head aside, and smiled in his spirit
a very bitter smile; and it struck the well-built wall.
And Telemachus rebuked Ctesippus with a word:

Ctesippus, truly this has turned out better for your spirit;
305	you did not hit the stranger; for he himself avoided the missile.
306	For I would have struck you in the middle with a sharp spear,
307	and instead of a wedding your father would have been busy with a funeral
308	here. So let no one show me unseemly acts
309	in the house; for I now understand and know each thing,
310	the good and the worse; before I was still a child.
311	But all the same we endure even this, looking on,
312	sheep being slaughtered and wine drunk
313	and bread; for it is hard for one to hold back many.
314	But come, no longer do me evils, being hostile;
315	and if you are already eager to kill me myself with bronze,
316	I would even wish that, and it would be much better
317	to be dead than to see these shameful deeds always,
318	strangers being mistreated and women servants
319	dragged about shamefully through the fair house.
So he spoke, and they all fell into silence, quiet;
and late Agelaus, son of Damastor, spoke among them:

Friends, no one would at a just saying
323	grow angry, assailing it with hostile words;
324	do not mistreat the stranger, nor any other
325	of the servants who are in the house of godly Odysseus.
326	And to Telemachus and his mother I would say a word
327	that is gentle, if it pleased the heart of you both.
328	As long as the spirit in your breasts hoped
329	that wise Odysseus would return to his own house,
330	so long there was no blame in waiting and holding back
331	the suitors in the house, since this was better,
332	if Odysseus returned and came back home;
333	but now this is already plain, that he is no longer to return.
334	But come, sit beside your mother and tell her this:
335	to marry whoever is the best man and gives the most,
336	that you may rejoice in having all your father's goods,
337	eating and drinking, and she may look after another's house.
Then prudent Telemachus answered him:

No, by Zeus, Agelaus, and by the sufferings of my father,
340	who somewhere far from Ithaca either has perished or wanders,
341	I do not delay my mother's marriage, but I bid her
342	marry whom she will, and I give countless gifts besides.
343	But I am ashamed to drive her unwilling out of the hall
344	with a word of compulsion; may a god not bring this to pass.
So spoke Telemachus; and on the suitors Pallas Athena
raised unquenchable laughter, and led their wits astray.
And they now laughed with jaws not their own,
and ate flesh smeared with blood; and their eyes
were filled with tears, and their spirit foreboded lamentation.
And among them spoke Theoclymenus, godlike:

Ah wretches, what evil is this you suffer? In night
352	are wrapped your heads and faces and the knees below.
353	Wailing is kindled, and your cheeks are wet with tears,
354	and with blood the walls and the fair panels are sprinkled;
355	full of ghosts is the porch, and full the courtyard,
356	hastening to Erebus beneath the gloom; and the sun
357	has perished out of heaven, and an evil mist has swept over.
So he spoke, and they all laughed sweetly at him.
And among them Eurymachus, son of Polybus, began to speak:

The stranger who has newly come from elsewhere is out of his wits.
361	But quickly, young men, send him out of the house
362	to go to the assembly, since here he finds it night.
Then Theoclymenus, godlike, spoke to him in turn:

Eurymachus, I do not bid you provide me escorts;
365	I have eyes and ears and both feet
366	and a mind in my breast made not at all ill;
367	with these I shall go out of doors, since I see an evil
368	coming upon you, which none of you suitors could escape or avoid,
369	you who in the house of godlike Odysseus
370	act insolently to men and devise wanton deeds.
So saying he went out of the well-inhabited house,
and came to Peiraeus, who received him with ready goodwill.
And the suitors all, looking at one another,
provoked Telemachus, laughing at the strangers;
and thus one of the overbearing young men would say:

Telemachus, no one is worse at entertaining guests than you;
377	what a one is this you have, a begging wanderer,
378	in need of food and wine, and not at all skilled
379	in works or in strength, but just a burden on the land.
380	And that other stood up to prophesy.
381	But if you would listen to me, it would be much better:
382	throw the strangers into a many-benched ship
383	and send them to the Sicilians, whence they would fetch you a worthy price.
So spoke the suitors; but he paid no heed to the words,
but silently looked at his father, always waiting
for when he would lay hands on the shameless suitors.
And she, having set her very beautiful chair opposite,
the daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope,
heard the speech of each man in the halls.
For they, laughing, had prepared their dinner,
sweet and satisfying, since they had sacrificed very many;
but no other supper could be more graceless
than that which a goddess and a strong man
were soon to set; for they had first devised shameful deeds.
